high.title: Hardcoded AES encryption key
high.description: The app stores a hardcoded AES key '0123456789!@#$%^' in the string resources, which is used to encrypt and decrypt password reset tokens.
high.impact: An attacker can recover this key from the APK to decrypt existing tokens or forge a valid token for any user (e.g., 'anniemaes@gmail.com') to bypass authentication and reset passwords.
high.recommendation: Use the Android Keystore system to generate and store encryption keys securely.

with.title: AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding encryption in NewPasswordActivity

high.title: Weak cryptography protects data that is locally extractable
high.description:
Two findings in this app combine into a single exploitable path: "AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding encryption in NewPasswordActivity" and "Hardcoded AES encryption key".

Attack path:
1. Attacker extracts hardcoded key from strings.xml
2. Attacker obtains encrypted data from local storage
3. Attacker applies the key and ECB mode as implemented in NewPasswordActivity to decrypt the data
high.impact: The encryption on the stored data is reversible - a hardcoded key in the app, or a mode that leaks structure - and the ciphertext is reachable without root. The encryption buys nothing.
high.recommendation: Use AES-GCM with a key generated in and held by the Android Keystore. A key compiled into the APK is public.

medium.title: AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding encryption in NewPasswordActivity
medium.description: The app uses 'AES' as the transformation string for the Cipher, which defaults to AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding on Android. ECB mode is insecure as it does not provide semantic security (identical plaintext blocks result in identical ciphertext blocks).

medium.title: Exported activity NewPasswordActivity has no permission protection
medium.description: Activity "edu.ksu.cs.benign.NewPasswordActivity" is reachable by any app on the device (Has an intent-filter and no explicit android:exported (implicitly exported)) and declares no permission. It handles NEWPASS. The NewPasswordActivity is exported and contains an intent-filter for 'edu.ksu.cs.benign.NEWPASS'. It allows access to the password reset screen if a valid 'token' extra is provided. Because the token is encrypted with a hardcoded key, any malicious app on the device can forge a token for 'anniemaes@gmail.com' and launch this activity to reset the password.
medium.impact: Any installed app can invoke this component and whatever it does with the data it is handed.
medium.recommendation: Set android:exported="false" if it is internal, or guard it with a signature-level permission and validate all input.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 27 those defaults still permit cleartext HTTP (see the cleartext finding).
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.

info.title: Sensitive screens not protected from capture
info.description: The app does not use FLAG_SECURE on activities that display sensitive information such as user emails or reset tokens.
info.impact: Sensitive data can be leaked via screenshots or screen recording apps.
info.recommendation: Set FLAG_SECURE in onCreate() for sensitive activities.

reasons: Screen contents not protected from capture. Without FLAG_SECURE, what a screen shows can end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview. That matters on screens showing credentials, card numbers or balances; on its own it is a hardening note.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 allows implicit component export
info.description: On targetSdk 27, any component with an intent-filter is exported unless it says otherwise.
info.recommendation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 31+ and declare android:exported explicitly on every filtered component.

reasons: Legacy platform behaviour from SDK levels. An SDK level is a statement about which platform defaults apply, not a defect. It is context for the findings that depend on those defaults - pair it with one of them.
warnings: Implicit export only applies below targetSdk 31; confirm the app's targetSdkVersion before treating this as exploitable.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 22 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "edu.ksu.cs.benign". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task.
info.impact: On a device running Android 10 or lower, a malicious app can put a look-alike screen on top of this app's task, phishing credentials or keeping the real app from being shown.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.
